raw_response:
I am fifty-eight years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou since I was a girl. I never went to school, but I know my land better than any book. I manage about eight mu with my family. Around here, if you do not plant winter wheat and summer maize, you are taking a big risk. The wheat gives us flour for our own steamed bread, and the maize always has a buyer at the village collection point. So this year, just like last year, I will put seven mu into the wheat–maize rotation. For the wheat, I will rotary-till the soil after the autumn rains and sow the improved “Liangxing” variety that my neighbor also uses. I will buy the special compound fertilizer from the shop—the shopkeeper knows which bags are for wheat—and topdress once in spring. I will irrigate four times: the winter irrigation is the most important, then three more times before harvest. After we cut the wheat in early June, there is no time to waste; I will plant the hybrid maize seeds directly without tillage, using the machine that comes to the village. Maize needs less water, so two irrigations are enough, but I will spray pesticides three times to keep the borers away. I will also keep one mu for cotton. It is hard work—my back hurts from bending to pick the bolls and from all the spraying—but the price per jin is better than maize, and I need the cash for medicine and for my grandchildren. I will rotary-till that plot in spring, sow the hybrid “Guoxin” cotton, and water it three times. The cotton needs a lot of pesticide, maybe a dozen times or more, because the aphids and bollworms never rest, but I have done it for twenty years and I know when to spray.
